quizzes.title: Recognition Criteria Practice (MCQ)
quizzes.passage: India runs a multi-party system, which the booklet contrasts with the one-party system of China and the two-party system of the USA. Parties are groups of like-minded individuals who voluntarily organise to gain political power through constitutional means and to promote the national interest. The Election Commission does not treat all parties alike. It classifies them as national parties or state parties, and each category is judged against its own set of criteria. Both categories are measured by the votes a party polls and the seats it wins at general elections to the Lok Sabha or the legislative assemblies. The booklet sets out the national party criteria first and the state party criteria after them. Across these tests, valid votes are counted either across several states or within a single state, and seats are counted either from one or more states, from a state's allotment, or in a state legislature. Recognised national and state parties are allotted a symbol that is exclusively reserved for their use in their respective jurisdiction. The booklet opens with a recent debate over the possible use of a cockroach as a political symbol, which drew attention to the framework governing election symbols. The booklet presents each category as a list of tests. Each test is written with a specific threshold, so the exact figures matter.

questions.q: What share of valid votes must a party poll in any four or more states at a general election to the LS or LA to qualify as a national party?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists 6% of valid votes in any four or more states as a national party criterion.

questions.q: From how many states must a national party win 2% of Lok Sabha seats at a general election?
questions.explanation: One national party criterion is winning 2% of LS seats at a general election from three states.

questions.q: Under the state party criteria, one Lok Sabha seat is required for every how many seats, or any fraction thereof, allotted to the state?
questions.explanation: A state party must win one LS seat for every 25 seats or any fraction thereof allotted to the state.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Recognition of a party as a national or state party is linked to its results at general elections.
Reason (R): Recognition is granted to parties that win seats in state assemblies, with no vote-share test attached.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The criteria include vote-share tests, so R is false while A is true.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. National party: valid votes in any 4 or more states   ->   D. 1 Lok Sabha seat
II. National party: Lok Sabha seats from one or more states   ->   A. 6% of valid votes
III. National party: Lok Sabha seat share from 3 states   ->   B. 4 Lok Sabha seats
IV. State party: Lok Sabha seats per 25 allotted seats   ->   C. 2% of Lok Sabha seats
questions.explanation: Each criterion pairs with its own figure: 6% in four or more states, 4 LS seats, 2% of LS seats from three states, and 1 LS seat per 25 seats.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A national party may qualify by winning 4 seats in the Lok Sabha from one or more states.
II. A state party may qualify by securing 6% of valid votes polled in the state at a general election to the LS from the state and winning 1 LS seat from that state.
III. Recognition under these criteria is based on valid votes polled and seats won at general elections to the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the booklet criteria, while III wrongly refers to Rajya Sabha elections instead of LS and LA elections.

questions.q:
Read the statements below:
1. A state party may qualify by securing 8% of the total valid votes polled in the state at a GE to the LS or LA.
2. A national party may qualify by being recognised as a state party in 2 states.
3. A state party may qualify by winning 3% of LA seats or 3 seats, whichever is more.
How many of the statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 match the booklet, while statement 2 wrongly gives 2 states instead of 4 for recognition as a state party in four states.

The booklet sets out the national party criteria first and the state party criteria after them. Across these tests, valid votes are counted either across several states or within a single state, and seats are counted either from one or more states, from a state's allotment, or in a state legislature. Recognised national and state parties are allotted a symbol that is exclusively reserved for their use in their respective jurisdiction. questions.q: How many Lok Sabha seats must a national party win from one or more states? (number)
questions.explanation: A national party must win 4 LS seats from one or more states.

questions.q: What percentage of total valid votes polled in a state must a state party secure at a general election to the LS or LA? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: One state party criterion is securing 8% of total valid votes polled in the state at a GE to the LS or LA.

questions.q: Under the state party criterion based on seats, what fixed minimum number of LA seats applies whichever is more than 3% of seats? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet sets the minimum at 3 LA seats, whichever is more than 3% of the seats.

questions.q: A state party wins one Lok Sabha seat for every how many seats, or any fraction thereof, allotted to the state? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet sets one LS seat for every 25 seats or any fraction thereof allotted to the state.

questions.q: How many Lok Sabha seats must a state party win from the state, along with securing 6% of valid votes in the state at a GE to the LS from that state? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet requires 6% of valid votes in the state at a GE to the LS plus one LS seat from the state.

questions.q: From how many states must a national party win 2% of Lok Sabha seats at a general election? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists winning 2% of LS seats at a general election from 3 states as a national party criterion.

questions.q: What percentage of valid votes must a national party secure in any four or more states at a general election? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The national party criterion requires 6% of valid votes in any four or more states.

quizzes.title: 1968 Order Practice (MCQ)
quizzes.passage: Election symbols are part of India's multi-party system, which the booklet contrasts with the one-party system of China and the two-party system of the USA. A political party is described as a group of like-minded individuals who voluntarily organise to gain political power through constitutional means and to promote the national interest. A recent debate over the possible use of a cockroach as a political symbol drew attention to the framework that governs election symbols in India. That framework is the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, which provides the legal basis for how symbols are reserved and allotted. Parties and candidates do not all stand on the same footing under it. Recognised parties, whether national or state, are placed differently from parties that are registered but not recognised, and both differ from independent candidates. The booklet presents the framework in a short list of key points, starting with the basic legal structure of the Order. Each group has its own position, and the booklet explains these positions in a compact, ordered form. The booklet also places its material in a current affairs format, with a historical example and a set of practice questions at the end. The booklet is published as part of a monthly current affairs series.

questions.q: Which body issued the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Order was issued by the Election Commission of India.

questions.q: Which of the following functions is NOT covered under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order?
options: Registration and recognition of political parties
Classification of parties as national or state parties
Resolution of disputes from party splits and mergers
questions.explanation: The booklet lists registration, classification and dispute resolution as coverage, but not regulation of campaign expenditure.

questions.q: How are free symbols allotted under the Order?
options: By the ECI from a notified list
By order of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The booklet says free symbols are allotted by the ECI from a notified list.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Order covers the classification of parties as national or state parties.
Reason (R): The Order covers the registration, recognition and derecognition of political parties.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are listed coverage items, but R about registration and derecognition does not explain the classification in A.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Classification of parties   ->   D. Registered unrecognised parties and independent candidates
II. Resolution of disputes from party splits   ->   A. National or state party categories
III. Source of free symbols   ->   B. Party splits and mergers
IV. Eligibility for free symbols   ->   C. A notified list
questions.explanation: Classification matches national or state categories, dispute resolution matches splits and mergers, free symbols come from a notified list, and eligibility covers registered unrecognised parties and independent candidates.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Order covers the resolution of disputes arising from party splits and mergers.
II. Independent candidates may be allotted reserved symbols under the Order.
III. Free symbols are available to registered unrecognised parties and independent candidates.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III match the booklet, while II is wrong because reserved symbols go only to recognised parties.

questions.q:
Read the statements below:
1. The Order covers the registration of political parties.
2. The Order covers the derecognition of political parties.
3. The Order covers the allotment of free symbols by the Supreme Court.
How many of the statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 match the booklet, while statement 3 is wrong because free symbols are allotted by the ECI.

questions.q: Which body issued the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order? (abbreviation)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Order was issued by the Election Commission of India, abbreviated ECI.

questions.q: What category of symbols is allotted by the ECI from a notified list? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says free symbols are allotted by the ECI from a notified list.

questions.q: Besides party splits, which other event does the Order's dispute resolution cover? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists resolution of disputes arising from party splits and mergers.

questions.q: Which function of the Order is the opposite of recognition? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists derecognition alongside registration and recognition as a function of the Order.

questions.q: Which function of the Order is the process of formally entering parties in the register? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists registration of political parties as one of the Order's functions.

questions.q: Which wing includes elected MPs, MLAs and MLCs in the ECI's party-split tests? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists the legislative wing as elected MPs, MLAs and MLCs, where applicable.

questions.q: In the Congress split example, what does the R in Congress (R) stand for? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet names Congress (R) as the Requisitionists faction that the ECI recognised after the split.
